title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
prompt:
Return the length of the longest **strictly increasing** subsequence of `nums`. A subsequence keeps order but may skip elements.

**Example**: `[10,9,2,5,3,7,101,18]` → `4` (e.g. `[2,3,7,101]`).

**Constraints**: `1 <= nums.length <= 2500`, `-10⁴ <= nums[i] <= 10⁴`.
hints: Suppose an increasing subsequence ends at `nums[i]`. What was its previous element, and what do you need to know about subsequences ending there?
Let dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i. dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i] (or 1 if there's none).
The answer is the max over all dp[i], not dp[n-1]. For O(n log n): keep a sorted `tails` list and binary-search each number into it.

solution.explanation: An increasing subsequence ending at i is either nums[i] alone or a longer one ending at a smaller nums[j] with j < i, extended by nums[i]. Checking every j finds the best. The overall LIS ends somewhere, hence the max over all i. O(n²) time, O(n) space. Patience sorting (binary search into a `tails` array) gets O(n log n).
